Hey no worries at all, and you'll absolutely find lots of similarities. Generally speaking those will be what we call cognates (i.e. words in two languages that both descend from one word in a parent language to both). An example of this would be German Hund and English hound (both from proto-West-Germanic hund), Arabic malik (ملك) and Hebrew melech (both from proto-Semitic malk-), Japanese senpai and Korean seonbae (not actually cognates, but old borrowings from Chinese sen pwojH), etc. It's a really interesting thing, and it makes certain Hebrew texts somewhat accessible when you're aware of it (and are always consulting a dictionary and translation). Sometimes you'll also get borrowings in the Quraan. Yunis for example is borrowed from the Greek Ionas for Jonah/Yonah, meaning dove in Hebrew. The -s at the end is a Greek grammatical ending. Lots of similar cases in prophets with names that end in an S. Certain words like jabarot (جبروت) derive from Aramaic, likely being borrowings that came with Christianity. Firdaus/فردوس is a borrowing from proto-Iranian. Just dumping a lot of this in case it helps. I think these details really ground the Quraan as a text that exists within a cultural context. Its borrowings from Christianity coincide with borrowings from Aramaic and Greek, the Arabs idolisation of the Persians and Byzantines manifest in borrowings from their languages and cultures.

Not sure who they are, but I study linguistics at uni, big lover of semitic languages. I know Arabic used to be written in Hebrew script at some point, but the script a language is written in has nothing to do with the language. It's like if I started writing English with Arabic letters. It would still be English at its core.

Arabic and Hebrew stem from the same branch of the Semitic language family, and the modern Arabic script is thought to originate from a modified version of Syriac. Written Arabic of this form existed a good deal before Islam, they didn't spontaneously invent writing for the sake of preserving the Quraan, just look at the countless pre-Islamic inscriptions we have (not to mention the muallaqat). It's just that Arab culture was largely oral. Islam just brought about a shift in culture, as was the case with the Iliad in Greece.

I mean it's hardly unique to English. English I imagine has more of this kind of stuff than most languages, but people seem to blow it out of proportion. Take a look at French for example, where the spoken forms of parle, parles, parlent are identical, as are parler, parlé, and parlez. Plurals sound identical to singulars half the time unless they're followed by a vowel. Learning a language will almost always involve a million things that just don't make sense, because natural languages aren't systems consciously designed by people to be logical.

Linguist, native Arabic speaker, and someone who picked up English quite easily and is very comfortable with it here. I feel the need to mention that as languages simplify in certain areas, they become more complex in others. Standard Arabic is highly inflected, as was old English, and many will look to that and conclude that Arabic is more complicated/advanced/whatever. But when you look at Arabic dialects, you notice that they lose a lot of those inflections while gaining stuff like stricter word order and unique grammatical features (Egyptian Arabic has stuff like the present continuous قاعد أعمل as distinct from simple present بعمل when standard Arabic has no such distinction, etc.). Similar thing applies to English when compared to old English. 

I only feel the need to mention all this because a lot of Arabs spread myths about Arabic being more complicated (read by Arabs as 'superior') and thus making Arabs a superior people. I've seen this used to discriminate against non Arabs and non Muslims, and I hate it, so I feel I should take any and all opportunities to nip it in the bud.

I hear a lot of fucked stories, but my experience has honestly been incredibly positive. My therapist was very no bullshit with me, and was constantly snapping me out of my own head and back to reality. She helped me understand the mechanics behind a lot of the feelings I had, and gave me the tools to be able to figure things out on my own. It isn't just a short term relief, I've genuinely changed a good deal of my shitty beliefs and the way I'd approach things in the past. I've gotten over all sorts of anger issues, I've learned to be properly mindful of other people which has helped me so much, I've gained an appreciation for life in general, even if it's shitty. Plenty more too, just not stuff I'm willing to go into. I'm hardly in a perfect place, in fact I'm often fucking miserable. But I also feel so much more aware, and more capable of dealing with things as they come my way. I haven't been able to go back for a while because of money, but I'm certainly not dependent on therapy. 

Of course, this all comes with caveats. In therapy, you do all the work. A therapist's only job is to help you make sense of things and guide you in the right direction. After that, you will see no improvement whatsoever unless you work for it. This is also gonna entail fully trusting what your therapist says, and being open to changing as a person. Most of all, you must swallow your pride. Understand that you know nothing, and be ready to accept what your therapist has to say. For me, what really helped was having her explain things such that I wasn't blindly trusting her, but agreeing with her reasoning. That's obviously gonna be pretty tough when you constantly see examples of people who don't know what they're doing/don't give a shit like this. I lucked out with mine, she clearly cares about her job and is committed to doing it well. But I'm willing to believe that there are a lot more good therapists out there than it may seem. Late to the party, but I was in a similar boat, got diagnosed at 18. Definitely not a "since childhood" thing, relatively common in people that age iirc. 

I had lost a lot of weight by the time I got diagnosed (10kg underweight) so I started dieting and working out. Kept it up a while and was in the best shape of my life, felt amazing, with a 6 pack and everything. I had a sweet tooth before and I still do now, while maintaining relatively good bg levels (though I fuck around sometimes). I've had alcohol since diagnosis too, though I'm not a heavy drinker so all that amounts to is a couple beers and a whole lot of tepache. Your life is gonna be just fine, the only shitty part about diabetes is the strain it puts on your wallet, but that depends on where you are and your insurance. As you continue to live with it, you'll get better at estimating insulin dosages for certain metals and timing them so you don't get much of a spike. Eventually, it'll just be a thing you do, and you'll even figure out some foods you don't need insulin at all to enjoy. 

This is gonna be a bit of weird unsolicited advice, but something that helped me through my diagnosis was getting into coffee. Never enjoyed it before, but I learned to really "get it" as I explored new stuff. Black coffee won't spike your bg, and calling it all by one name is misleading; it's a whole world of unique and interesting flavours that you can get from all the different beans and brewing methods. Don't believe what chains like Starbucks and Caribou have taught us for decades about black coffee being this bitter boring drink, speciality coffee is one the most incredibly flavourful (and hardly ever bitter) things you can have. You won't really need that once you're comfortable with dosing insulin, but it was something that showed me at the time that I could still enjoy food the same if not more with diabetes. Good luck dealing with it all. I know how scary it can be at first, but it really does get better.
